{{short description|Triangle center}}

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''Clawson point''' is a special point in a [[triangle]] defined by the [[trilinear coordinates]] {{math|tan ''α'' :  tan ''β'' : tan ''γ''}},<ref name="etc2"/> where {{mvar|α, β, γ}} are the interior angles at the triangle vertices {{mvar|A, B, C}}. It is named after [[John Wentworth Clawson]], who published it 1925 in the [[American Mathematical Monthly]]. It is denoted ''X''(19) in [[Clark Kimberling]]'s [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]].

The Clawson point, the [[orthocenter]], the [[mittenpunkt]] and the [[Spieker center]] are collinear.<ref name="etc2"/>

== Geometrical constructions ==
There are at least two ways to construct the Clawson point, which also could be used as coordinate free definitions of the point. In both cases you have two triangles, where the three lines connecting their according vertices meet in a common point, which is the Clawson point.

=== Construction 1 ===
[[File:Clawson punkt3.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|
'''Construction 1:''' Clawson point as a homothetic center
{{legend-line|solid black|Reference triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|dashed grey 2px|[[Extended side]]s of {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid black 1px|[[Excircle]]s of {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid red|[[Orthic triangle]] {{math|△''H{{sub|A}}H{{sub|B}}H{{sub|C}}''}}, and triangle {{math|△''T{{sub|A}}T{{sub|B}}T{{sub|C}}''}}, internally [[tangent]] to each pair of excircles}}
{{legend-line|dashed red 2px|Perspective lines between {{math|△''H{{sub|A}}H{{sub|B}}H{{sub|C}}''}} and {{math|△''T{{sub|A}}T{{sub|B}}T{{sub|C}}''}}, which are [[Similarity (geometry)|similar]]; meet at the [[homothetic center]] {{mvar|P}} (the '''Clawson point''')}}
]]
For a given triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}, let {{math|△''H{{sub|A}}H{{sub|B}}H{{sub|C}}''}} be its [[orthic triangle]] and {{math|△''T{{sub|A}}T{{sub|B}}T{{sub|C}}''}} the triangle formed by the outer tangents to its three [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle|excircles]]. These two triangles are similar and the Clawson point is their [[center of similarity]], therefore the three lines {{mvar|T{{sub|A}}H{{sub|A}}, T{{sub|B}}H{{sub|B}}, T{{sub|C}}H{{sub|C}}}} connecting their vertices meet in a common point, which is the Clawson point.<ref name="ck"> [[Clark Kimberling]]: ''Central Points and Central Lines in the Plane of a Triangle.'' In: ''Mathematics Magazine'', Volume 67, no. 3, 1994, pp. 163–187, in particular 175. ([https://www.jstor.org/stable/2690608 JSTOR]).</ref><ref name="mw">{{MathWorld|title=Clawson Point|urlname=ClawsonPoint}} (retrieved 2019-11-30) </ref>

=== Construction 2===
[[File:Clawson punkt2.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|
'''Construction 2:''' Clawson point as a center of perspective
{{legend-line|solid #994c1a|Reference triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|dashed #994c1a 2px|[[Extended side]]s of {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid black 1px|[[Circumcircle]] and excircles of {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid blue|Triangle {{math|△''A'B'C',''}} formed by lines connecting pairs of [[Intersection (geometry)#Two circles|intersection points]] between each excircle and the circumcircle}}
{{legend-line|dashed red 2px|Perspective lines between {{math|△''ABC''}} and {{math|△''A'B'C',''}} meeting at the [[perspective center]] {{mvar|P}} (the '''Clawson point''')}}
]]

For a triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}, its circumcircle intersects each of its three excircles in two points. The three lines through those points of intersections form a triangle {{math|△''A'B'C'.''}} This triangle and {{math|△''ABC''}} are perspective triangles with the Clawson point being  their [[perspective center]]. Hence the three lines {{mvar|AA', BB', CC'}} meet in the Clawson point.<ref name="etc2"/>

== History ==
The point is now named after J. W. Clawson, who published its trilinear coordinates 1925 in the American Mathematical Monthly as problem 3132, where he asked for geometrical construction of that point.<ref name="clawson">J. W. Clawson, Michael Goldberg: ''problem 3132.'' In: ''The American Mathematical Monthly'', Volume 33, no. 5, 1926, pp. 285–285. ([https://www.jstor.org/stable/2299573 JSTOR)] </ref> However the French mathematician
[[Émile Lemoine]] had already examined the point in 1886.<ref name="etc1">Clark Kimberling: [https://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/encyclopedia/ETC.html#X19 ''X(19)=CLAWSON POINT'']. In: [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]] (retrieved 2019-11-30)</ref> Later the point was independently rediscovered by R. Lyness and G. R. Veldkamp in 1983, who called it ''crucial point'' after the Canadian math journal Crux Mathematicorum in which it was published as problem 682.<ref name="etc2">Clark Kimberling: [https://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/tcenters/recent/clawpt.html ''CLAWSON POINT'']. In: [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]] (retrieved 2019-11-30)</ref>
